goals: Distinguish the emf of a cell from its terminal potential difference and derive E = I(R + r)
Find the current from series, parallel and mixed groupings of cells, and from two unequal cells in parallel

slides.narration: Switch on a torch with weak cells and the bulb glows dimly, even though each cell is still rated one and a half volts. The cell itself has resistance, and some of its energy is used up inside it. In this part we separate the emf of a cell from the voltage at its terminals, learn how to group cells for the most current, and meet Kirchhoff’s two laws for networks.

slides.heading: Electromotive force (emf)
slides.body_md:
A cell uses chemical energy to move charge from its negative to its positive terminal, against the electric field inside it. The **emf** E is the work done by the cell per unit charge taken once round the complete circuit:
$$E = \dfrac{W}{q}\qquad(\text{unit: J C}^{-1} = \text{V})$$
bullets: Emf is not a force: it is energy supplied per coulomb.
On open circuit (no current) the terminal p.d. equals E.

slides.narration: Inside a cell, chemical reactions push positive charge towards the positive terminal, against the field. The energy the cell gives to each coulomb that goes once round the circuit is its electromotive force, or emf, measured in joules per coulomb, that is volts. Despite the old name, emf is not a force. When no current is drawn, a voltmeter across the cell reads exactly its emf.

slides.heading: Internal resistance and terminal potential difference
slides.body_md:
The electrolyte and electrodes have an **internal resistance** r. With an external resistor R, energy conservation per coulomb gives
$$E = IR + Ir = I(R + r),\qquad V = IR = E - Ir$$
bullets: **Ir** is the “lost volts”: energy per coulomb turned to heat inside the cell.
While the cell is being **charged** (current forced in at the + terminal): $V = E + Ir$.

slides.narration: Each coulomb that goes round gains E joules in the cell and gives up I R joules in the external resistor and I r joules inside the cell. So E equals I times R plus r. The terminal potential difference, the voltage across the external resistor, is E minus I r: the more current drawn, the lower it falls. When a charger forces current backwards through a cell, the terminal voltage is E plus I r instead.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a battery under load
slides.body_md: A battery of emf 4.5 V and internal resistance 0.30 Ω is connected to a 2.7 Ω resistor. Find the current, the terminal p.d. and the lost volts.
bullets: Step 3 — lost volts $Ir = 0.45$ V, heating the battery.

visual.alt: Worked table: current 1.5 amperes, terminal voltage 4.05 volts, lost volts 0.45 volt

slides.narration: The total resistance in the loop is three ohms, so four and a half volts drives one and a half amperes. Inside the battery, one and a half amperes through point three ohm uses up nearly half a volt, so the terminals show only about four point zero five volts. Checking, one and a half amperes through two point seven ohms gives the same answer.

slides.heading: Terminal p.d. against current
slides.body_md: Plotting V against I for one cell gives a straight line $V = E - Ir$:
bullets: Intercept on the V-axis (I = 0): the emf E.
Slope: −r. Intercept on the I-axis: the short-circuit current E/r.
Measuring V at two currents gives both E and r.

visual.alt: Terminal potential difference of a cell of emf 2 volts and internal resistance 0.4 ohm against the current it supplies: a straight line falling from 2 volts at zero current to zero at the short-circuit current of 5 amperes
visual.caption: Intercept on the V-axis = E; slope = −r.

slides.narration: If we vary the external resistance and plot the terminal voltage against the current, we get a straight line falling with slope minus r. Where it meets the voltage axis, at zero current, it gives the emf. Where it meets the current axis, at zero terminal voltage, is the short-circuit current, E over r. Two readings of voltage and current are enough to find both E and r.

slides.heading: Grouping identical cells
slides.body_md: Cells are grouped to give more voltage, more current or a longer life:
bullets: **Series** helps when R is large compared with r.
**Parallel** helps when R is small compared with r, and shares the load so the cells last longer.

visual.alt: Table of the equivalent emf, internal resistance and current for identical cells in series, in parallel and in mixed grouping

slides.narration: Join n identical cells in series and the emfs add, but so do the internal resistances. Join m in parallel and the emf stays the same while the internal resistance falls to r over m. Series wins when the external resistance is large; parallel wins when it is small, and each cell then supplies only a share of the current, so the battery lasts longer.

slides.heading: Mixed grouping: the best arrangement
slides.body_md:
N = mn cells as **m rows** in parallel, each of **n cells** in series:
$$I = \dfrac{nE}{R + \dfrac{nr}{m}}$$
bullets: For fixed N, I is **largest when** $R = \dfrac{nr}{m}$: the external resistance equals the internal resistance of the combination.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: twelve cells, one load
slides.body_md: Twelve cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.60 Ω, drive current through a 1.8 Ω resistor. Find the best grouping and the current. Compare all in series and all in parallel.
bullets: Best: $R = \dfrac{nr}{m}$ with $mn = 12$: $1.8 = \dfrac{0.6n}{m}$ gives $n = 3m$, so $3m^2 = 12$: **m = 2 rows of n = 6**.
All in series: $\dfrac{18}{1.8 + 7.2} = 2.0$ A; all in parallel: $\dfrac{1.5}{1.8 + 0.05} \approx 0.81$ A.

x.label: number of parallel rows m (12 cells in all)

visual.alt: Current through a 1.8 ohm load from twelve cells of 1.5 volts and 0.6 ohm each, against the number of parallel rows: 2.0 amperes with all in series, a maximum of 2.5 amperes with two rows of six, and only about 0.81 ampere with all twelve in parallel
visual.caption: Best arrangement: R = nr/m (here 1.8 Ω = 6 × 0.6/2).

slides.narration: Setting the load equal to the battery’s internal resistance, and keeping twelve cells in all, gives two rows of six. Each row has nine volts and three point six ohms; two rows in parallel have one point eight ohms. Nine volts across three point six ohms in total gives two and a half amperes, more than the two amperes from all in series and far more than the point eight from all in parallel.

slides.heading: Two cells of unequal emf in parallel
slides.body_md:
Cells $E_1, r_1$ and $E_2, r_2$ with positive terminals joined act as one cell of
$$E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2},\qquad r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$$
bullets: Derived from $V = E_1 - I_1r_1 = E_2 - I_2r_2$ and $I = I_1 + I_2$.

slides.heading: Kirchhoff’s laws
slides.body_md:
**Junction law** (conservation of charge): at any junction, $\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$, or $\sum I = 0$.

**Loop law** (conservation of energy): round any closed loop, $\sum E = \sum IR$, or the algebraic sum of potential changes is zero.

rows: through R in the direction of I

visual.alt: Sign convention table for Kirchhoff’s loop law: minus I R along the current, plus I R against it, plus E from the negative to the positive terminal of a cell, minus E the other way

slides.narration: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in a steady circuit, so what flows in must flow out: that is the junction law. A charge taken round any closed loop returns to its starting potential, so the rises and falls of potential cancel: that is the loop law, a statement of energy conservation. Assume a direction for each current; if one comes out negative, it simply flows the other way.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Work per unit charge by the cell; equals V on open circuit
$E = I(R + r)$, $V = E - Ir$; charging: $V = E + Ir$
Junction: charge conserved; loop: energy conserved

visual.alt: Summary table of emf, the cell on load, grouping of cells, unequal cells in parallel and Kirchhoff’s laws

slides.narration: To sum up: emf is the energy a cell gives each coulomb, and the terminal voltage falls below it by I r when current is drawn. Identical cells in mixed grouping give the most current when the load equals the internal resistance of the battery. Unequal cells in parallel act as one equivalent cell. And Kirchhoff’s junction and loop laws, from conservation of charge and energy, solve any network.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Derive $E = I(R + r)$ from energy per coulomb, not from a formula.
Charging or discharging? It decides $E - Ir$ or $E + Ir$.
In Kirchhoff problems, mark directions first and keep one sign convention.
A negative answer means the current flows opposite to your arrow; do not change the equations.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Examiners like the derivation of E equals I times R plus r from energy conservation, so practise it. Always ask whether the cell is charging or discharging before writing the terminal voltage. In network problems, draw and label every current first, then use one sign convention throughout. A negative current is not a mistake; it just flows the other way.

slides.narration: A meter that draws current always disturbs what it measures. The instruments in this part avoid that: they are balanced until a sensitive galvanometer reads zero. The Wheatstone bridge and its laboratory form, the metre bridge, measure resistance this way, and the potentiometer measures emf without drawing any current from the cell. All three follow directly from Kirchhoff’s laws.

slides.heading: The Wheatstone bridge
slides.body_md:
Four resistors P, Q, R, S, a cell across AC and a galvanometer across BD. At **balance** ($I_g = 0$), B and D are at the same potential, so the same current $I_1$ flows through P and Q and $I_2$ through R and S:
$$I_1P = I_2R,\quad I_1Q = I_2S\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$$
bullets: Loop ABDA with $I_g = 0$ gives the first equation; loop BCDB the second.
Balance does not depend on the emf of the cell or the resistance of the galvanometer.

slides.narration: In a Wheatstone bridge, the galvanometer joins the midpoints of two potential dividers. When it reads zero, no current crosses from B to D, so P and Q carry the same current, and so do R and S. The loop law round the left triangle gives I one P equals I two R, and round the right triangle I one Q equals I two S. Dividing, P over Q equals R over S.

slides.heading: The metre bridge
slides.body_md:
A practical Wheatstone bridge: a uniform wire 100 cm long forms the ratio arms. With X in the left gap and a known R in the right, balance at length l gives
$$\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad X = R\,\dfrac{l}{100 - l}$$
bullets: The wire’s resistance is proportional to length, so the arms are in the ratio l : (100 − l).
Choose R so that l is near the **middle**: the end resistances at the copper strips then matter least.
Touch the jockey gently; do not slide it along the wire.

slides.narration: In the metre bridge, the two lower arms of the bridge are replaced by the two parts of a uniform wire, one metre long, on either side of a sliding contact called the jockey. Their resistances are in the ratio of their lengths. So at balance, the unknown over the known resistance equals l over one hundred minus l. A balance near the middle of the wire gives the most reliable result.

slides.heading: The potentiometer: principle
slides.body_md:
A long uniform wire AB carries a **steady current** from a driver cell. The potential drop along it is proportional to length: $V = kl$. A cell joined (+ to A) through a galvanometer to a jockey is **balanced** at length l when its emf equals the drop over l:
$$E = kl$$
bullets: At balance **no current** flows through the cell, so its full emf is measured: the potentiometer is an **ideal voltmeter** (infinite resistance).
Needs: driver emf greater than E, and both + terminals joined to A.

slides.narration: A steady current through a uniform wire makes the potential fall evenly along it. Connect a cell, positive to A, through a galvanometer to a point on the wire. If the drop along the wire up to that point equals the emf, nothing flows through the galvanometer. Because the cell then supplies no current, there is no lost voltage inside it, and we measure its true emf.

slides.heading: Potential gradient
slides.body_md:
The **potential gradient** k is the fall of potential per unit length of the wire:
$$k = \dfrac{V_{AB}}{L} = \dfrac{I\rho}{A}\quad(\text{V m}^{-1})$$
bullets: k is constant along the wire only if the current is steady and the wire uniform (same material and cross-section).
The wire is made of an alloy such as constantan or manganin: high resistivity and very small temperature coefficient.

visual.alt: Potential drop along a uniform potentiometer wire against the length from end A: a straight line of slope 0.4 volt per metre, so a 1.08 volt cell balances at 2.7 metres and a 1.44 volt cell at 3.6 metres
visual.caption: Uniform wire, steady current: V ∝ l.

slides.narration: The potential gradient is the voltage across the whole wire divided by its length, or, equivalently, the current times the resistance of one metre of the wire. It is constant only if the current stays steady and the wire is uniform. That is why potentiometer wires are made of alloys like constantan, whose resistance hardly changes as they warm up.

slides.narration: The driver sends two volts through ten ohms, so the current is a fifth of an ampere and the wire, eight ohms, has one point six volts across it. Spread over four metres, that is a gradient of point four volt per metre. A Daniell cell of one point zero eight volts therefore balances two point seven metres from A.

slides.heading: Sensitivity of a potentiometer
slides.body_md: A potentiometer is more **sensitive** when a small change in emf gives a large change in balancing length, i.e. when **k is small**.
bullets: Use a **longer wire** (for the same p.d. across it).
Increase the **rheostat resistance** to reduce the current (but keep $kL > E$).
For a few millivolts (a thermocouple), a large series resistance makes k about a millivolt per metre.

visual.alt: Potential drop along a uniform potentiometer wire against the length from end A: a straight line of slope 0.4 volt per metre, so a 1.08 volt cell balances at 2.7 metres and a 1.44 volt cell at 3.6 metres
visual.caption: Uniform wire, steady current: V ∝ l.

slides.narration: Sensitivity means how far the balance point moves for a small change in emf. Since the length is emf divided by k, a smaller gradient spreads the same emf over more wire. We lower k by using a longer wire or by adding resistance in the driver circuit. But the whole wire must still carry more potential drop than the emf being measured, or there will be no balance point.

slides.heading: Comparing the emfs of two cells
slides.body_md:
With a two-way key, cells $E_1$ and $E_2$ are balanced in turn against the same wire (same k):
$$E_1 = kl_1,\quad E_2 = kl_2\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}$$
bullets: k cancels, so neither the driver emf nor the wire’s resistance needs to be known.
Internal resistances do not matter: no current flows through the cells at balance.

Each is balanced in turn against the same wire carrying the same current. Since each emf is k times its balancing length, the ratio of the emfs is just the ratio of the lengths, whatever the gradient.

slides.heading: Internal resistance of a cell
slides.body_md:
Balance the cell on open circuit ($K_2$ open): $E = kl_1$. Close $K_2$ so it drives current through R: the balance gives its terminal p.d. $V = kl_2$. Since $\dfrac{E}{V} = \dfrac{R + r}{R}$,
$$r = R\left(\dfrac{l_1 - l_2}{l_2}\right)$$
bullets: $l_2 < l_1$, because the terminal p.d. is less than E while the cell supplies current.

Now the balance measures the terminal voltage, which is smaller, so the balancing length is shorter. The ratio E over V equals R plus r over R, which rearranges to r equals R times l one minus l two, over l two.

slides.heading: Potentiometer or voltmeter?
slides.body_md: Why the potentiometer measures emf better:
columns:
**Potentiometer**
- No current at balance
- True emf
- Sensitivity adjustable

**Voltmeter**
- Draws current
- Terminal p.d. only
- Quick, but less accurate

rows: Reads the terminal p.d. (less than E)
Sensitivity raised by a smaller gradient k

visual.alt: Table comparing a potentiometer and a voltmeter for measuring the emf of a cell

slides.narration: A voltmeter always draws some current, so across a cell it reads the terminal voltage, a little less than the emf. The potentiometer draws none at balance, so it measures the emf itself, and its sensitivity can be raised by lowering the gradient. Its drawbacks are that it is slower to use and needs a steady driver cell.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: $X = R\,l/(100 - l)$; balance near the middle
$E = kl$ at balance; no current drawn

slides.narration: To sum up: a Wheatstone bridge balances when the ratios of its arms are equal, and the metre bridge uses the two parts of a uniform wire as two of those arms. A potentiometer balances an emf against the steady potential drop along a uniform wire, drawing no current, so it compares emfs by the ratio of lengths and finds internal resistance from two balancing lengths.

If no balance point exists, suspect a weak driver cell or a cell connected the wrong way round. sections.heading: 1. Emf, internal resistance and terminal p.d.
sections.body_md:
- **Emf** E: work done by the cell (non-electrostatic, chemical action) per unit charge taken once round the circuit; unit volt (J C⁻¹). Equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit.
- **Internal resistance** r: resistance of the electrolyte and electrodes; grows with electrode separation, falls with larger immersed area.
- Energy per coulomb: $E = IR + Ir = I(R + r)$, so the **terminal p.d.** $V = IR = E - Ir$ while discharging; $V = E + Ir$ while being charged.
- V–I graph: straight line, intercept E on the V-axis, slope −r, short-circuit current E/r (e.g. E = 4.5 V, r = 0.30 Ω, R = 2.7 Ω: I = 1.5 A, V = 4.05 V).

key_terms.definition_md: Energy supplied by a source per unit charge passing once round the circuit.
Resistance of the material inside a cell, through which its own current must pass.

sections.heading: 2. Grouping of cells
sections.body_md:
- **n identical cells in series:** emf nE, resistance nr; $I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr}$ (best when R ≫ r). With some cells reversed, their emfs subtract but their resistances still add.
- **m identical cells in parallel:** emf E, resistance r/m; $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r/m}$ (best when R ≪ r).
- **Mixed (m rows of n):** $I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr/m}$, largest when $R = nr/m$.
- **Two unequal cells in parallel:** $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2}$, $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$. The weaker cell may be charged by the stronger one.

sections.heading: 3. Kirchhoff’s laws
sections.body_md:
- **Junction law** (conservation of charge): $\sum I = 0$ at any junction.
- **Loop law** (conservation of energy): $\sum E = \sum IR$ round any closed loop.
- Signs: −IR going along the current through a resistor, +IR against it; +E crossing a cell from − to +, −E from + to −.
- Assume directions; a negative answer means the current flows the other way. Use as many independent loops as there are unknown currents less the junction equations.

sections.heading: 4. Wheatstone bridge and metre bridge
sections.body_md:
- Wheatstone bridge (P, Q in one pair of arms, R, S in the other, galvanometer between their junctions): **balanced** when $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$ (from the loop law with $I_g = 0$). Balance is independent of the cell’s emf and the galvanometer’s resistance; the bridge is most sensitive when all four arms are of the same order.
- **Metre bridge:** uniform 100 cm wire forms two arms; unknown X in the left gap, known R in the right, balance at l: $X = R\,\dfrac{l}{100 - l}$. Aim for l near 50 cm (end resistances matter least); interchange X and R and average.

sections.heading: 5. Potentiometer: principle, gradient, sensitivity
sections.body_md:
- A uniform wire carrying a steady current: potential drop ∝ length, $V = kl$. A cell (+ to A) balanced at length l: $E = kl$, with **no current** drawn — an **ideal voltmeter**.
- **Potential gradient** $k = V_{AB}/L = I\rho/A$ (V m⁻¹). Wire of constantan or manganin (high ρ, low temperature coefficient), uniform cross-section.
- **Sensitivity** rises as k falls: longer wire, more resistance in the driver circuit. Balance needs driver emf (p.d. across the wire) > E and both + terminals at A.

key_terms.definition_md: Fall of potential per unit length along the potentiometer wire.
Change in balancing length per unit change in emf; greater when the potential gradient is smaller.

sections.heading: 6. Potentiometer applications
sections.body_md:
- **Comparing emfs** (two-way key, same k): $\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}$; neither k nor the internal resistances are needed. Sum-and-difference method: $\dfrac{E_1 + E_2}{E_1 - E_2} = \dfrac{l_a}{l_b}$.
- **Internal resistance:** open circuit $E = kl_1$; with R across the cell, $V = kl_2$; $r = R\,\dfrac{l_1 - l_2}{l_2}$.

questions.stem_md: The emf of a cell is best described as

options.text_md: the force with which the cell pushes electrons round the circuit
the potential difference across its terminals while it supplies a large current
the total charge the cell can deliver before it runs down
the work done by the cell per unit charge in taking charge once round the complete circuit

questions.solution_md: Emf is energy supplied per coulomb (J C⁻¹ = V), not a force; it equals the terminal p.d. only when no current flows — option (d).

questions.stem_md: When a cell supplies no current, an ideal voltmeter connected across its terminals reads the ___ of the cell.
questions.solution_md: The **emf**: with I = 0 there are no lost volts, so V = E − Ir = E.

questions.stem_md: A 9.0 V battery delivers 0.50 A to a radio, and its terminal potential difference is then 8.2 V. Find the internal resistance of the battery, in ohms.
A 12 V battery of internal resistance 0.40 Ω lights a lamp of resistance 5.6 Ω. Find the potential difference across the terminals of the battery, in volts.
A cell drives 0.40 A through a 4.0 Ω resistor and 0.20 A through a 9.0 Ω resistor. Find the emf of the cell, in volts.

A charger drives a current of 8.0 A into a 12 V car battery of internal resistance 0.050 Ω (entering at its positive terminal). The potential difference across the battery terminals during charging is
questions.solution_md: While charging, the charger must supply the emf plus the drop across r: V = E + Ir = 12 + 8.0 × 0.050 = 12.4 V — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A thick copper strip of negligible resistance joined across the terminals of a 1.5 V dry cell carries 3.0 A. The internal resistance of the cell is

options.text_md: zero

questions.solution_md: With R ≈ 0 only r limits the current: I = E/r, so r = 1.5/3.0 = 0.50 Ω — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For a cell supplying current to a variable resistor, the graph of its terminal potential difference against the current is a straight line sloping downwards.

**Reason (R):** The internal resistance of a cell increases in proportion to the current drawn from it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: V = E − Ir with E and r constant, a line of slope −r. R is false: r is (nearly) constant — that is why the graph is straight — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the emf of a cell and the potential difference across its terminals while it supplies current.

answer.model_answer_md: **Emf** is the energy the cell supplies per coulomb, fixed whatever the current. **Terminal p.d.** is the energy per coulomb delivered to the external circuit, $V = E - Ir$, so it falls as the current rises and is **less than the emf**, equal to it only on open circuit.

questions.solution_md: Energy supplied versus delivered; V = E − Ir < E.

marking_scheme.step: Emf: energy supplied per coulomb, independent of current
Terminal p.d.: depends on I, V = E − Ir < E

questions.stem_md: A cell of emf E and internal resistance r drives a steady current I through an external resistor R. Using conservation of energy, derive E = I(R + r), and hence write the terminal potential difference.

answer.model_answer_md: In time t a charge $q = It$ goes once round the circuit. The cell does work $W = Eq = EIt$ on it. This energy is dissipated as heat in R, $I^2Rt$, and in the cell’s own resistance, $I^2rt$. Energy conservation: $EIt = I^2Rt + I^2rt$, so $E = I(R + r)$. The terminal p.d. is the p.d. across R: $V = IR = E - Ir$.

questions.solution_md: Work by the cell equals heat in R and r.

marking_scheme.step: Work by cell EIt for charge It
Equated to I²Rt + I²rt: E = I(R + r)

questions.stem_md: State two factors on which the internal resistance of a cell depends. Why does a torch with old cells give a dim light although the cells still show nearly 1.5 V on a high-resistance voltmeter?

answer.model_answer_md: Internal resistance **increases** with the **separation of the electrodes** and **decreases** with the **area of the electrodes** in the electrolyte (it also falls as the electrolyte warms). An old cell has a **large r**: its emf is nearly unchanged, but on load the lost volts **Ir** are large, so the bulb gets a small terminal p.d.

questions.solution_md: Factors; large r gives large lost volts on load.

marking_scheme.step: Two factors (electrode separation, immersed area, temperature)
Old cell: large r, so large Ir on load

questions.stem_md: Five identical cells, each of emf E and internal resistance r, are joined in series and connected to an external resistance R. The current in R is
questions.solution_md: In series the emfs add (5E) and so do the internal resistances (5r): I = 5E/(R + 5r) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Four identical cells, each of emf E and internal resistance r, are joined in parallel with their positive terminals together. The combination behaves as a single cell of

options.text_md: emf 4E and internal resistance r/4
emf E and internal resistance 4r
emf E/4 and internal resistance r/4
emf E and internal resistance r/4

questions.solution_md: Each cell has the same emf, so the common emf is E; four equal resistances in parallel give r/4 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Six identical cells are to send the largest possible current through a resistor whose resistance is much smaller than the internal resistance of one cell. The cells should be joined

options.text_md: all in series
as two parallel rows of three in series
all in parallel
as three parallel rows of two in series

questions.solution_md: I = nE/(R + nr/m) with nm = 6; for R ≪ r the current ≈ mE/r, largest for m = 6, n = 1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A battery is made of m parallel rows, each of n identical cells (internal resistance r each) in series. For a fixed total number of cells, the current in an external resistance R is greatest when

options.text_md: R = mr/n
R = mnr
R = nr/m
R = r

questions.solution_md: I = nE/(R + nr/m) = NE/(mR + nr); with mR × nr = NRr fixed, the denominator is least when mR = nr, i.e. R = nr/m: the external resistance equals the internal resistance of the battery — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Eight cells, each of emf 2.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω, are arranged in two parallel rows of four cells in series, and connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find the current in the resistor, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: Each row: emf $4 \times 2.0 = 8.0$ V, resistance $4 \times 1.0 = 4.0$ Ω; two rows in parallel: 8.0 V and 2.0 Ω. $I = \dfrac{8.0}{2.0 + 2.0} = 2.0$ A.

questions.stem_md: Sixteen cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω, are to be grouped in equal parallel rows to drive the largest possible current through a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find this largest current, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: Largest current when $R = \dfrac{nr}{m}$ with $mn = 16$: $2.0 = \dfrac{0.50n}{m}$, so $n = 4m$ and $4m^2 = 16$: $m = 2$ rows of $n = 8$. $I = \dfrac{8 \times 1.5}{2.0 + 8 \times 0.50/2} = \dfrac{12}{4.0} = 3.0$ A.

questions.stem_md: A battery of six cells in series, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.20 Ω, is assembled with two of the cells connected the wrong way round. It is connected to a 3.8 Ω resistor. Find the current, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: Net emf $= (4 - 2) \times 1.5 = 3.0$ V (each reversed cell cancels a correct one); internal resistance still $6 \times 0.20 = 1.2$ Ω. $I = \dfrac{3.0}{3.8 + 1.2} = 0.60$ A.

questions.stem_md: A 6.0 V battery of internal resistance 1.0 Ω and a 4.0 V battery of internal resistance 2.0 Ω are connected in parallel, positive terminal to positive terminal. Find the emf of the equivalent single battery, in volts (3 significant figures).
Five identical cells, each of emf 1.2 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω, are joined in parallel and connected to a 0.80 Ω resistor. Find the current in the resistor, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: Parallel: emf 1.2 V, resistance $\dfrac{1.0}{5} = 0.20$ Ω. $I = \dfrac{1.2}{0.80 + 0.20} = 1.2$ A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When one cell of a series battery is connected the wrong way round, the internal resistance of the battery decreases.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The reversed cell’s emf subtracts (the battery loses 2E), but its internal resistance is still in series, so the total resistance is unchanged.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two cells of unequal emf joined in parallel, with no external load, gradually run down.

**Reason (R):** A current circulates between them, the cell of larger emf driving charge backwards through the cell of smaller emf.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the circulating current (E₁ − E₂)/(r₁ + r₂) wastes energy as heat in both internal resistances — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Explain why identical cells are joined in parallel, rather than in series, when the external resistance is much smaller than the internal resistance of each cell.

answer.model_answer_md: In series, n cells give emf nE but also resistance nr, so with R ≪ r the current is **nE/nr = E/r**, no better than one cell. In parallel the emf stays E but the resistance falls to **r/m**, so the current approaches **mE/r**, m times larger; each cell also supplies only **1/m** of it.

questions.solution_md: Series adds r as fast as E; parallel divides r.

questions.stem_md: N identical cells, each of emf E and internal resistance r, are arranged in m parallel rows of n cells in series and connected to an external resistance R. Obtain the current in R and show that it is maximum when R = nr/m.

answer.model_answer_md: Each row has emf $nE$ and resistance $nr$; m equal rows in parallel give emf $nE$ and resistance $\dfrac{nr}{m}$. So $I = \dfrac{nE}{R + nr/m} = \dfrac{mnE}{mR + nr} = \dfrac{NE}{mR + nr}$. With N fixed, I is largest when $mR + nr$ is least. Since $(mR)(nr) = NRr$ is constant, the sum $mR + nr = (\sqrt{mR} - \sqrt{nr})^2 + 2\sqrt{NRr}$ is least when $mR = nr$, i.e. $R = \dfrac{nr}{m}$.

questions.solution_md: Equivalent battery; minimise the denominator.

marking_scheme.step: Row emf nE, battery resistance nr/m

questions.stem_md: Two cells of emfs E₁ and E₂ and internal resistances r₁ and r₂ are connected in parallel, positive to positive, across a resistance R. Obtain expressions for the emf and internal resistance of the equivalent cell.

answer.model_answer_md: Let the cells supply $I_1$ and $I_2$, with $I = I_1 + I_2$ through R, and let V be the common terminal p.d. Then $V = E_1 - I_1r_1 = E_2 - I_2r_2$, so $I_1 = \dfrac{E_1 - V}{r_1}$, $I_2 = \dfrac{E_2 - V}{r_2}$. Adding: $I = \dfrac{E_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{E_2}{r_2} - V\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$, which rearranges to $V = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2} - I\,\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$. Comparing with $V = E_{eq} - Ir_{eq}$: $E_{eq} = \dfrac{E_1r_2 + E_2r_1}{r_1 + r_2}$, $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$.

questions.solution_md: Common V; add currents; compare with V = E − Ir.

questions.stem_md: While applying Kirchhoff’s loop law, you pass through a cell of emf E (negligible internal resistance) from its positive terminal to its negative terminal. The term you write for the cell is

questions.stem_md: Two batteries share a load. A 12 V battery in series with 3.0 Ω and a 6.0 V battery in series with 3.0 Ω are connected in parallel, positive terminals together, across a 6.0 Ω load. Find the current in the load, in amperes.

questions.stem_md: Explain how Kirchhoff’s junction law follows from conservation of charge and how his loop law follows from conservation of energy.

answer.model_answer_md: **Junction:** in a steady state charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so the charge flowing in per second equals that flowing out: **ΣI = 0**. **Loop:** the electrostatic field is conservative, so a charge taken round a closed loop returns to the same potential; the energy gained from emfs equals that lost in resistors: **ΣE = ΣIR**.

questions.solution_md: No pile-up of charge; zero net potential change round a loop.

marking_scheme.step: Loop: potential (energy per charge) returns to its value

questions.stem_md: Three branches are joined between points X and Y: a 9.0 V cell in series with 3.0 Ω, a 6.0 V cell in series with 6.0 Ω (both cells with negligible internal resistance and positive terminals towards X), and a 6.0 Ω resistor. Use Kirchhoff’s laws to find the current in each branch, and comment on the result for the 6.0 V cell.

answer.model_answer_md:

Solving: $I_1 = 1.0$ A, $I_2 = 0$, $I_3 = 1.0$ A, with $V_X - V_Y = 6.0$ V. The p.d. across the 6.0 V branch equals its emf, so **no current** flows through that cell: it neither charges nor discharges.

questions.solution_md: Two loop equations and the junction law.

from B to D, because B is at the higher potential
nowhere, because the bridge is balanced
from B to D only if the emf of the cell is large enough

answer.model_answer_md: At balance B and D are at the **same potential** and **no current** flows through the galvanometer, so its resistance never enters the equations. questions.stem_md: Using Kirchhoff’s laws, derive the condition for balance of a Wheatstone bridge with resistances P (AB), Q (BC), R (AD) and S (DC), a cell across A and C and a galvanometer across B and D.

answer.model_answer_md: At balance the galvanometer current is zero, so by the junction law the current $I_1$ in P also flows through Q, and the current $I_2$ in R also flows through S. Loop ABDA (no emf, $I_g = 0$): $I_1P - I_2R = 0$, so $I_1P = I_2R$. Loop BCDB: $I_1Q - I_2S = 0$, so $I_1Q = I_2S$. Dividing: $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$.

questions.solution_md: Junction law with I_g = 0, two loops, divide.

marking_scheme.step: I_g = 0: same current in P and Q, in R and S
Loop equations I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S

no current is drawn from the cell

questions.stem_md: A potentiometer wire 5.0 m long has a resistance of 10 Ω. It is connected in series with a 15 Ω resistance box and a 2.0 V accumulator of negligible internal resistance. Find the potential gradient along the wire, in V m⁻¹.

options.text_md: the jockey is pressed too firmly on the wire
the potentiometer wire is longer than necessary
the galvanometer is too sensitive
the potential difference across the whole wire is less than the emf being measured

questions.solution_md: A null point needs kL > E (and both + terminals at A). If the drop across the whole wire is smaller than E, the galvanometer current never reverses — option (d).

questions.stem_md: To make a potentiometer able to distinguish between two cells whose emfs differ by only a few millivolts, the experimenter should

options.text_md: reduce the resistance in series with the driver cell, raising the potential gradient
increase the resistance in series with the driver cell, reducing the potential gradient
replace the wire with a shorter one of the same material
use a driver cell of larger emf with no series resistance

questions.stem_md: The driver of a potentiometer is an accumulator of negligible internal resistance connected directly across the wire, with no rheostat. The wire is replaced by one of the same material and cross-section but twice as long. The balancing length for a given cell

options.text_md: halves
doubles
is unchanged
becomes four times as long

questions.solution_md: The whole driver emf is still across the wire, now twice as long, so k halves and l = E/k doubles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The fall of potential per unit length along a potentiometer wire carrying a steady current is called the potential ___.
questions.solution_md: The potential **gradient** k (V m⁻¹).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Increasing the resistance of the rheostat in the driver circuit of a potentiometer increases the balancing length for a given cell.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At its balance point a potentiometer behaves like a voltmeter of infinite resistance.

**Reason (R):** At the balance point no current flows in the branch containing the cell and the galvanometer.

Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.stem_md: On a 10 m potentiometer wire the potential gradient is 0.25 V m⁻¹. At what length from the positive end will a cell of emf 1.10 V balance? Give the answer in metres.

A 10 m potentiometer wire of resistance 20 Ω is to measure thermocouple emfs of a few millivolts, so its potential gradient must be 10 mV per metre. The driver is a 2.0 V accumulator of negligible internal resistance. What resistance must be connected in series with the wire? Give the answer in ohms.
questions.solution_md: P.d. across the wire $= 0.010 \times 10 = 0.10$ V, so $I = \dfrac{0.10}{20} = 0.0050$ A. Total resistance $= \dfrac{2.0}{0.0050} = 400$ Ω, so the series resistance is $400 - 20 = 380$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: Why is a potentiometer wire made of an alloy such as constantan, and why must it have a uniform cross-section along its length?

answer.model_answer_md: Constantan has a **high resistivity**, giving a usefully large p.d. across the wire, and a **very small temperature coefficient**, so k stays steady as the current warms it. A **uniform cross-section** (and material) makes the resistance per unit length the same everywhere, so the **potential drop is proportional to length**.

questions.solution_md: High ρ, small α; uniform resistance per length.

marking_scheme.step: Alloy: high resistivity, small temperature coefficient
Uniform: V ∝ l along the wire

questions.stem_md: A student finds that two cells of nearly equal emf balance at almost the same point on a potentiometer. Suggest two ways of making the instrument distinguish them better, giving a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Reduce the **potential gradient** k: (1) increase the **resistance of the rheostat** in the driver circuit, lowering the current; (2) use a **longer wire** with the same driver. Since **l = E/k**, a smaller k makes a given difference in emf give a **larger difference** in balancing length.

questions.solution_md: Smaller k, larger change in l.

marking_scheme.step: Two ways: more rheostat resistance, longer wire
Reason: l = E/k, smaller k spreads the difference

questions.stem_md: Explain why a potentiometer is preferred to a moving-coil voltmeter for measuring the emf of a cell. State one disadvantage of the potentiometer.

answer.model_answer_md: A voltmeter must take **some current** from the cell to deflect, so it reads the **terminal p.d.** E − Ir, which is less than E. A potentiometer is a **null method**: at balance **no current** is drawn, so there are no lost volts and the **true emf** is measured; it acts as a voltmeter of **infinite resistance**, and its sensitivity can be raised by **reducing k**. Disadvantage: it is **slower** to use and needs a **steady driver** cell.

questions.solution_md: Null method draws no current.

marking_scheme.step: Voltmeter draws current: reads E − Ir
Potentiometer: no current at balance, true emf (infinite resistance)
One disadvantage (slow, needs steady driver, not portable)

questions.stem_md: Why must the positive terminals of the driver cell and of the cell under test be connected to the same end of the potentiometer wire?

answer.model_answer_md: Only then does the test cell’s emf **oppose** the potential drop along the wire between A and the jockey. At one point the two become **equal** and the galvanometer current is zero. If the cell were reversed, its emf would **add** to the drop and the galvanometer would deflect the same way everywhere: **no null point**.

questions.solution_md: Opposition is needed for a null point.

marking_scheme.step: Emf must oppose the drop along the wire
Otherwise they add: no null point

questions.stem_md: On a potentiometer, a standard cell of emf 1.02 V balances at 272 cm and a dry cell at 400 cm. Find the emf of the dry cell, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{E_x}{E_s} = \dfrac{l_x}{l_s}$, so $E_x = 1.02 \times \dfrac{400}{272} = 1.50$ V.

questions.stem_md: Two cells are joined in series and balanced on a potentiometer: with their emfs aiding each other the balancing length is 4.5 m, and with them opposing it is 1.5 m. The ratio of the larger emf to the smaller is

increases, because the terminal p.d. rises

questions.stem_md:

questions.stem_md: Describe how a potentiometer is used to find the internal resistance of a cell, and derive r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂, where l₁ and l₂ are the balancing lengths without and with a resistance R across the cell.

answer.model_answer_md: The cell (+ to A) is joined through a galvanometer to the jockey, with a resistance box R and key $K_2$ across it. With $K_2$ open the cell supplies no current and balances at $l_1$: $E = kl_1$. With $K_2$ closed it drives current I through R, and the balance at $l_2$ gives the terminal p.d.: $V = IR = kl_2$. questions.stem_md: Explain, with the circuit described in words, how a potentiometer with a two-way key is used to compare the emfs of a Leclanché cell and a Daniell cell. State one precaution.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the emf and the internal resistance of a cell, and use conservation of energy to show that its terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir. (b) $5.6 = E - 2.0r$ and $5.9 = E - 0.50r$: subtracting, $0.30 = 1.5r$, so $r = 0.20$ Ω and $E = 5.6 + 2.0 \times 0.20 = 6.0$ V.

(c) Charging: $V = E + Ir = 6.0 + 2.0 \times 0.20 = 6.4$ V.

questions.stem_md: In a car, the generator, the battery and a headlamp are connected in parallel between two points X and Y. answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Junction law: the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum leaving (conservation of charge). Loop law: round any closed loop the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the IR products (conservation of energy).

(b) Let $V = V_X - V_Y$. Junction X: $\dfrac{15 - V}{0.50} + \dfrac{12 - V}{1.0} = \dfrac{V}{9.0}$, i.e. $42 = V\left(2 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{9}\right)$, so $V = 13.5$ V. (c) $V_X - V_Y = 13.5$ V, more than the battery’s emf, so the generator drives 1.5 A into it: the battery is **charging**.

questions.stem_md: (a) State the principle of the potentiometer and explain why it is said to act as an ideal voltmeter. [1] (b) A 6.0 m potentiometer wire of resistance 9.0 Ω is in series with a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 V driver of negligible internal resistance. Find the potential gradient. [1] (c) A cell balances at 5.00 m on open circuit and at 4.00 m when a 6.0 Ω resistor is connected across it. Find its emf and internal resistance. [2] (d) Can a 2.0 V cell be balanced on this arrangement? If not, what change would allow it? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
